clauses.why: An org-wide kill switch is an operational control the request does not call for; removing grants or the bot suffices.
Restoring an org-wide switch exists only because the spec introduced that switch.
A detailed failure taxonomy for administrators goes beyond showing that an attempt failed.
Revision rollback is a lifecycle capability beyond creating the bot.
Starting disabled depends on the spec-introduced org-wide enable switch.
A local readiness view of setup blockers is an administrative feature the request does not need.
A data-egress disclosure to users is not required for a development-org Grok bot to work.
Late or duplicate outcome suppression arises from the spec's own client deadline and redelivery model.
Behaviour of in-flight requests under org-wide disablement exists only because of the spec's kill switch.
Withholding an already-fetched reply after mid-flight revocation is extra engineering beyond admission checks.
Atomic lifecycle guarantees for update and rollback go beyond creating the bot.
Revision tracking for administrators belongs to the spec-introduced update/rollback lifecycle.
Salesforce Apex heap limits are 6 MB synchronous and 12 MB asynchronous, not 10 MB and 25 MB; this also conflicts with C-63.
A distinct size-related failure category belongs to the extra diagnosis taxonomy; bounded context rarely nears Grok's window.
Classifying throttling as a named capacity failure is part of the extra diagnosis taxonomy.
Administrator identification of xAI billing restrictions is diagnostic tooling beyond the request.
Production deployment is outside the request's development-org scope.
Production coverage requirements are outside the request's development-org scope.
Production trigger coverage requirements are outside the request's development-org scope.
Production specified-test coverage is outside the request's development-org scope.
Describing xAI audit retention to users is a disclosure duty the request does not call for.
Update, rollback and removal are spec-introduced lifecycle operations beyond creating the bot.
Capping displayed entries at 20 is unnecessary; follow-up context is already bounded by C-32.
Distinguishing disabled, setup-needed and outbound failures relies on the extra taxonomy and kill switch.
Separating provider credential rejection from Salesforce access failure is part of the extra diagnosis taxonomy.
Model-specific setup failure identification is part of the extra diagnosis taxonomy.
A named temporary-failure category is part of the extra diagnosis taxonomy.
A fallback category exists only because the spec introduced a failure taxonomy.
Per-category recovery instructions build on the extra diagnosis taxonomy.
A supported removal procedure is lifecycle tooling beyond creating the bot.
Rollback semantics exist only because the spec introduced revision rollback.
Rollback semantics exist only because the spec introduced revision rollback.
Removal semantics exist only because the spec introduced bot removal.
Invalidating views across revisions arises only from the spec's update/rollback lifecycle.
Clearing the visible conversation on detected revocation is extra behaviour beyond refusing new sends.
Blocking replies to obsolete views arises only from the spec's revision lifecycle.
Context timing against eviction arises only from the extra 20-entry display cap.
A consolidated settings inspection view, including enabled state, is administrative tooling beyond the request.
A rejected settings write leaving the old value in effect is true of any transactional Salesforce settings save.
Multi-blocker feedback involves spec-introduced blockers like obsolete views and the disabled state.
Production deployment is outside the request's development-org scope.
Update-retention semantics belong to the spec-introduced revision lifecycle.
Update-retention semantics belong to the spec-introduced revision lifecycle.
Arises only from the spec's revision replacement and rollback lifecycle.
Idempotent handling of redelivered submissions is extra engineering the request does not need.
